description: From read-through to opening night: how directors, performers and designers shape a production.
content_html:
The Journey from Script to Stage

A script is a set of instructions written by a playwright, but it is not a performance. The gap between the words on the page and a live audience sitting in a darkened theatre is filled by the rehearsal process: weeks or months of collaborative work in which the director, performers, and designers translate the playwright’s intentions into concrete theatrical choices. Understanding the stages of that process — and who is responsible for what at each stage — prepares you to write convincingly about how theatre is made and why it looks and sounds the way it does.

Key Fact

The main stages of a professional rehearsal process are: read-through (the whole company reads the script together for the first time), blocking rehearsals (the director sets the performers’ movement), character and scene work (performers and director develop character depth), production meetings (director and designers align their choices), technical rehearsal (first run in the theatre with all technical elements), dress rehearsal (full run as if performing to an audience), and previews (early performances with a paying audience before opening night).

The Read-Through and Early Rehearsals

The read-through is not a performance — it is a first shared encounter with the text. The director typically introduces the production’s concept at this stage: what world the play will live in, what the central questions are, and what the company is trying to communicate to the audience. Designers may present models and mood boards. Performers begin to form a relationship with their character’s language, but no choices are fixed at this stage.

Early rehearsals are exploratory. The director works scene by scene, often asking performers to try different interpretations: different blocking choices, different emotional approaches, different vocal and physical reads of the same line. This is the phase in which the director discovers whether their concept works in practice, and whether the performers can find genuine truth within it. A director might ask a performer to try playing a scene entirely in stillness, then try it with continuous movement, to find out which communicates more clearly to an audience at the back of the house.

Production Meetings

A production meeting brings the director, designers, stage manager and heads of department together to co-ordinate. At a production meeting the director might clarify that a particular scene requires a lighting special on a specific person from above, or that a costume needs to allow a performer to move extremely quickly. The designer comes back with a solution. Everything discussed is recorded by the stage manager in the production notes, which feed into the prompt copy. Production meetings happen throughout the rehearsal period, not just at the start.

The prompt copy (sometimes called the book) is the most important document in a production. It records every blocking decision, every technical cue — the exact word or action at which the lighting state changes, the sound plays, the flown piece descends — and every note made during rehearsals. During a performance, the stage manager follows the prompt copy and uses it to call cues over the headset system. If the stage manager loses their place, the production is in immediate danger.

Each technical department also produces cue sheets. The lighting operator has a cue sheet listing every lighting state change (LX Q1, LX Q2...) with the moment it occurs and the instruction (fade to black over 3 seconds; snap to lighting state 7). The sound operator has an equivalent document. These cue sheets are prepared by the designer and the stage manager together during and after technical rehearsals.

The Technical Rehearsal

The technical rehearsal (the “tech”) is the first time the production runs with all its elements together: the set, lighting, sound, costumes, props and performers, in the actual theatre. It is notoriously slow. The stage manager calls a cue; the operator runs it; the director watches from the auditorium and gives notes. A single scene of three minutes may take an hour to tech because a lighting state may need refocusing, a sound cue may arrive at the wrong moment, or a scene change may need to be refined. The performers must hit their blocking precisely because the lighting has been focused for specific positions — stand in the wrong place and you will be in darkness or shadow.

Dress Rehearsal and Previews

The dress rehearsal is a full performance run, as close to opening night as possible. Notes are given by the director afterwards but the run is not usually stopped. The purpose is to allow the company to perform the production from first scene to last without intervention, building stamina and confidence. For the stage manager, it is a final check that all cues are in the right place and every transition is smooth.

Previews are early performances with a paying audience, before the production’s official opening night. The audience’s responses in preview — where they laugh, where they are silent, where they seem confused — give the director valuable information. Changes are often made after previews: blocking adjusted, a scene cut, a cue repositioned. Many productions are substantially different on opening night from what they were on the first preview.

Key Fact

The technical rehearsal is the first run with all technical elements in the theatre; it is slow and stop-start, pausing to fix each cue. The dress rehearsal is a continuous run in full performance conditions; it is as close to a real performance as possible. Both come before opening night. Previews (with audiences) come after the dress rehearsal but before opening night.

Questions that ask you to “explain how a director and performers work together” or “describe the stage manager’s contribution to a production” are testing knowledge of the rehearsal process. A common error is to treat theatre as a spontaneous activity — to write as if performers make choices moment by moment in front of an audience. Professional theatre is painstakingly planned. Every lighting cue has been rehearsed. Every piece of blocking has been set. Every sound cue has been placed at a specific moment. The spontaneity the audience experiences is the result of hundreds of rehearsed decisions executed simultaneously. When you write about staging choices in extended-response answers, you are implicitly writing about rehearsal choices: decisions made in advance, tested, refined, and locked in place.
exam_tip_html: Questions about the rehearsal process often ask for named stages or the role of a specific person at a specific stage. For 1-mark and 2-mark questions, name the correct stage (read-through, blocking, tech rehearsal, dress rehearsal, preview) and be precise about who is accountable for what. For 4-mark questions, describe a stage, explain what happens at it, and link it to the production’s quality or the audience’s experience. For extended-response (12 or 20 marks) questions that ask you to “direct a production” or “stage a scene”, you are implicitly writing as a rehearsal director — every staging decision you describe is a decision that would have been rehearsed and refined before opening night. Using rehearsal vocabulary (blocking, production meeting, tech, prompt copy) signals to the examiner that you understand how professional theatre actually works, and this raises your answer into the Mastering or Secure band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The rehearsal process moves from read-through (first encounter with the text) through blocking, scene work and production meetings, to the technical rehearsal (first run with all elements), dress rehearsal (full continuous run), and previews (early performances with a paying audience).
  • The stage manager holds the prompt copy — the authoritative record of every blocking and cue decision — and calls all cues during performances. The production meeting co-ordinates all departments and is chaired by the director.
  • Every staging choice in a professional production has been rehearsed, refined and locked. When you write about staging in exam answers, you are writing about rehearsal decisions — using rehearsal vocabulary signals professional understanding.

practice_questions.text: What is the first stage of a professional theatre rehearsal process called?
What is blocking in the context of theatre rehearsal?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that blocking is the pattern of movement a performer makes around the stage; 1 mark for explaining that blocking is set by the director during rehearsals and recorded in the prompt copy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a technical rehearsal and a dress rehearsal, and what each stage contributes to the production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately describing the technical rehearsal (first run in the theatre with all technical elements, stop-start to fix cues); 1 mark for accurately describing the dress rehearsal (full continuous run in performance conditions, as close to opening night as possible); 1 mark for explaining what the tech contributes (co-ordination of all technical departments, refinement of cue timings); 1 mark for explaining what the dress rehearsal contributes (stamina and confidence for the company; final check that transitions are smooth; a director's last chance for major notes before the audience arrives).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a production meeting contributes to the success of a production, and what the stage manager's role is within it.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for explaining that a production meeting brings director and all design/technical departments together to co-ordinate; 1 mark for giving a specific example of what is discussed or resolved (e.g. the director clarifies where a lighting special must fall; the set designer confirms the delivery date for a piece of scenery; a costume quick-change problem is identified and solved); 1 mark for the stage manager's role (records all decisions in the production notes, which feed into the prompt copy; circulates action points to departments); 1 mark for linking the production meeting to the audience's eventual experience (if departments are not aligned, the production fails technically in front of an audience — production meetings prevent this).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the collaboration between a director and a sound designer during the rehearsal process might shape the audience's experience of a specific scene. In your answer, refer to at least one stage of the rehearsal process and specific sound design choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the collaboration between director and sound designer is analysed through at least one named rehearsal stage (e.g. production meeting where director establishes the emotional intention of a scene; tech rehearsal where the sound cue is placed precisely at the moment a character makes a turning-point decision); specific sound choices named (e.g. a low-frequency drone building under a confrontation scene; a sudden sharp silence on the word of revelation; a diegetic sound cue of distant traffic that is gradually removed to create isolation); the intended effect on the audience is precisely stated and connected to the director's intention.

Secure: collaboration described through at least one rehearsal stage; specific sound choices present; audience effect described; directorial intention generally linked.

Developing: rehearsal process referenced but not used analytically; sound choices are generic; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic description of sound design with no rehearsal process reference; audience effect absent.

practice_questions.text: As a director, describe the decisions you would make during rehearsals to stage a key scene that involves a sudden reversal of power between two characters. Refer to specific choices from at least two disciplines (performer and one design role) and explain how you would develop these choices through the rehearsal process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clearly defined power reversal; specific performer choices developed through named rehearsal stages (e.g. in blocking the powerful character begins downstage centre with the other character upstage; as rehearsals progress the reversal is staged as a physical crossing — the characters swap spatial positions — timed to a specific line); specific design choices from one discipline (e.g. lighting: a cross-fade from a warm state favouring one character to a cold state favouring the other, refined during tech rehearsal); the rehearsal process is used meaningfully (choices are developed and changed during rehearsals, not simply presented as final); the combined effect of performance and design is discussed.

Secure: power reversal identified; performer and design choices present with some specificity; at least one rehearsal stage referenced; audience effect described.

Developing: staging ideas described but limited connection to rehearsal process; design or performance choices are general; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic staging description with no rehearsal process vocabulary; power reversal not clearly staged; audience effect absent.

knowledge_checks.q: At which stage of the rehearsal process does the full company sit together and read the script aloud for the first time?
What is the main purpose of a technical rehearsal?
options: To give the performers a chance to perform without stopping in front of an invited audience
To run all technical elements in the theatre for the first time, pausing to fix cues and co-ordinate departments
To allow the director to give final notes after the last preview
To rehearse the read-through with the full company, designers and stage management present

knowledge_checks.q: The pattern of movement a performer makes around the stage, set by the director during rehearsals and recorded in the prompt copy, is called _____.
The _____ is the master copy of the script held by the stage manager, containing all blocking, cues and creative decisions.
Match each rehearsal stage to what primarily happens there:
right: First shared encounter with the text; the director introduces the concept
First run with all technical elements; slow and stop-start to fix cues
Full continuous run in performance conditions; no stops except in an emergency

flashcard_questions.q: What is the read-through in professional theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The first stage of rehearsal where the whole company reads the script aloud together.
The pattern of movement a performer makes around the stage, set by the director in rehearsal.
The master script held by the stage manager recording all blocking, cues and creative decisions.
A regular meeting between director and all design/technical departments to co-ordinate the production.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a technical rehearsal and a dress rehearsal?
flashcard_questions.a: Tech is stop-start to fix cues; dress is a full continuous run in performance conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: What are previews in professional theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: Early performances with a paying audience before the official opening night.

flashcard_questions.q: What document lists every lighting or sound cue in performance order for the operator?
Why does a performer need to follow their blocking precisely during the technical rehearsal?
flashcard_questions.a: The lighting has been focused for specific positions — standing in the wrong place puts the performer in darkness.

flashcard_questions.q: Who calls all technical cues during a live performance?
flashcard_questions.a: The stage manager, using the prompt copy and speaking into headsets worn by operators.

flashcard_questions.q: What information might a director gain from previews that they could not get from a dress rehearsal?
flashcard_questions.a: A real audience's responses — where they laugh, fall silent or seem confused — allowing last changes before opening night.

flashcard_questions.q: In the rehearsal process, what does 'locking' a choice mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Finalising a decision so all departments can plan around it — changes after a lock have technical consequences.

glossary_terms.definition: The first stage of the rehearsal process, in which the whole company reads the script aloud together.
The pattern of movement a performer makes around the stage, set by the director during rehearsals and recorded in the prompt copy.
A regular meeting between the director and all design and technical departments to co-ordinate progress and ensure every element of the production is aligned.
The master copy of the script, held by the stage manager, containing all blocking, stage directions, technical cues and creative decisions recorded during the rehearsal process.
Documents listing every technical cue for a department in the order they occur in the performance, with the cue number, trigger and operational instruction.
A rehearsal held in the performance space with the full technical production elements operating for the first time, used to co-ordinate all technical cues with the performers.
A full run of the production in performance conditions, with costumes, make-up, all technical elements and the full cast, as a final preparation before opening to the public.
